a.s: Sive objects to the match but is too isolated to act, so her death in the bog becomes a silent protest against the life chosen for her.

b.s: once Desdemona is accused in Othello, she can only protest her innocence and submit, and her dying words, 'Nobody; I myself', shield the husband who has killed her.

link.why: Both young women are silenced by the people around them, and neither can save herself by speaking out.

a.s: Mike cannot look his mother in the face when he insists the match is for the best, yet he says nothing to stop it.

b.s: Emilia finally breaks her silence in Othello, defying her husband's orders and Othello's sword to reveal the truth about the handkerchief.

link.why: Mike's silence keeps a wrong going, while Emilia risks, and loses, her life to speak the truth.

a.s: In Sive, a matchmaker, an aunt and an uncle settle a schoolgirl's marriage for £200, as if she were goods to be sold.

b.s: women are treated as property in Othello, where Iago wakes Brabantio by shouting 'thieves!' and telling him to look to his house, his daughter and his bags.

link.why: In both societies a young woman is treated as a possession of the men and families around her.

a.s: In Sive, no guard, court or official ever appears, and a private bargain made in a kitchen decides a girl's life.

b.s: Venice offers a fair hearing in Othello, as the Duke lets Othello and Desdemona speak before dismissing Brabantio's charge of witchcraft.

link.why: Sive's world has no law to turn to, while Venice's institutions at first listen to both sides.

a.s: In Sive, goodness exists in Liam, Nanna and the travelling men, but it is powerless against the money that drives the match.

b.s: goodness in Othello is real but cannot save itself, as Desdemona stays loyal to the end and Emilia dies defending her mistress's honour.

link.why: Both plays show good people defeated, which is a large part of what makes their visions so bleak.

a.s: In The Shawshank Redemption, Andy crawls through five hundred yards of sewer pipe and stands in the pouring rain with his arms raised, finally free.

b.s: the only escape left to Sive is death in the bog, because Liam's letter offering her a way out is burned before she can read it.

link.why: Andy's escape leads to freedom and life, while Sive's only way out of her trap is death.

a.s: Liam is the one character in Sive who speaks out openly, but when he begs Mike and Mena to stop the match, they simply send him away.

b.s: Andy's courage pays off in The Shawshank Redemption: by daring to speak up to Captain Hadley on the roof, he wins beer for his fellow workers.

link.why: Both men find the courage to speak to those with power, but only Andy's words change anything.

a.s: At Shawshank, Captain Hadley beats a frightened new prisoner to death on Andy's first night, and no one is held to account.

b.s: than Hadley's violence, threats keep the weak in line in Sive, where Mena and Thomasheen silence Nanna by threatening her with the county home.

link.why: Both worlds silence the powerless, but Sive's bullies use threats where Shawshank's guards use open violence.

a.s: In Sive, Carthalawn's mocking songs comment on the action like a chorus, telling the truth about greed and foreshadowing a death.

b.s: in The Shawshank Redemption, Red's voiceover guides how we feel, taking us from his warning that hope is dangerous to the film's last words, 'I hope'.

link.why: Both texts use a voice that stands slightly outside the action to shape how the audience sees the story.

a.s: In Sive, every glimmer of hope, from Liam's secret visit to his escape plan, is crushed by the adults' greed.

b.s: than Sive, The Shawshank Redemption admits that hope can be crushed, as Brooks hangs himself after his release and Tommy is killed for being willing to tell the truth.

link.why: Both texts show hope destroyed, but in the film these losses are outweighed by Andy's escape, while in Sive nothing outweighs them.

a.s: In Small Things Like These, Bill holds out his empty hands to the girl in the chapel who begs for his help, saying it is not up to him.

b.s: Bill, Mike in Sive stays silent when he could act, doing nothing to warn Sive after Thomasheen burns Liam's letter.

link.why: Both men see a wrong being done and at first do nothing, so their silence makes them complicit.

a.s: In Sive, Mena uses Sive's birth outside marriage as a weapon, telling her she will have no name till she takes a husband.

b.s: than Sive, Small Things Like These shows how unmarried mothers are punished: Sarah's baby is taken from her and she is locked away in the convent.

link.why: Both societies shame unmarried mothers, but Keane shows it through cruel words while Keegan shows girls locked up and babies taken.

a.s: In Sive, the Church stays in the background as a source of rules and respectability, and no priest ever steps in to protect Sive.

b.s: than in Sive, the Church holds real power in Small Things Like These, where the nuns run the laundry and the best girls' school.

link.why: Religion shapes respectability in both worlds, but only in Keegan's New Ross does the Church directly control people's lives.

a.s: Small Things Like These ends with Bill walking Sarah home through the town, feeling a happiness greater than any he has known.

b.s: Sive ends with a drowned girl, a lament and Nanna's grief, while those who profited from the match slip away unpunished.

link.why: Keegan's ending offers hope through one man's courage, while Keane's leaves only grief and injustice.

a.s: Keane's play opens in a cramped, poor kitchen full of insults and resentment, where the schoolgirl Sive is treated as a burden.

b.s: Small Things Like These opens in a cold, struggling town, where businesses are closing, people are emigrating and Bill worries about money.

link.why: Both openings show a world worn down by poverty, which casts a shadow over the outlook from the start.

a.s: In Othello, Iago, who holds no high rank, uses cunning to destroy a good man, turning Desdemona's goodness into 'the net / That shall enmesh them all'.

b.s: in The Shawshank Redemption, Andy uses his cleverness against a corrupt man, turning the false identity he invented to hide Norton's money into a way of taking that money himself.

link.why: Both men overturn someone more powerful through cleverness, but Iago's power destroys the innocent while Andy's brings down the guilty.

a.s: In The Shawshank Redemption, prison traps Brooks's mind as well as his body: after fifty years he is 'institutionalized' and cannot cope with the free world.

b.s: Othello becomes a prisoner of his own mind: once Iago's suggestions take hold, he cannot go back to trusting Desdemona, and he bids 'Farewell the tranquil mind!'

link.why: In both texts the worst trap is inside a man's own head, and neither man escapes it.

a.s: In Othello, the Duke gives Othello and Desdemona a fair hearing before dismissing Brabantio's charge of witchcraft.

b.s: the Venetian Senate, the court in The Shawshank Redemption fails Andy completely, convicting him of two murders he did not commit.

link.why: Venice's institutions first show justice working, while the film opens with the law condemning an innocent man.

a.s: The Shawshank Redemption says almost nothing directly about race: Red is a Black man and Andy a white former banker, but the film never makes race an issue.

b.s: than The Shawshank Redemption, Othello makes race part of its world: racist language greets Othello from the first scene, when Iago calls him 'an old black ram'.

link.why: Both texts have a Black central character, but only Othello shows a society that openly judges a man by his colour.

a.s: In Othello, Iago reveals his plan to the audience in soliloquy while Othello keeps calling him 'honest Iago', so we watch the disaster coming, helpless to stop it.

b.s: Darabont hides Andy's escape from the viewer as well as from Red, so its sudden reveal gives us the same shock and delight.

link.why: Shakespeare lets us see the evil coming, which fills us with dread, while Darabont keeps the good news secret, which lifts us.

a.s: In Small Things Like These, Bill knows he will pay for taking Sarah out of the convent, yet he chooses his conscience over his family's security.

b.s: than Bill, Emilia pays for speaking out in Othello: she reveals the truth about the handkerchief and is stabbed by her own husband.

link.why: Both characters' courage has a cost, but Emilia pays with her life while Bill's price lies in an uncertain future.

a.s: In Small Things Like These, Bill asks whether the nuns have only as much power as people give them, suggesting that their control depends on the town's silence.

b.s: Othello, where Iago's power depends on others trusting him as 'honest Iago' and never questioning what he tells them.

link.why: In both texts power is not simply held but given by others, and it lasts only as long as no one challenges it.

a.s: Authority in Othello lies with the state: the Duke and Senate judge Brabantio's complaint, and a letter from Venice can recall even a great general.

b.s: the real authority in Small Things Like These is the Catholic Church, and even a respected businessman like Bill treads carefully around the Mother Superior.

link.why: Power in Venice belongs to the state, while in Keegan's town it belongs to the Church.

a.s: At the end of Othello, Iago refuses to explain himself, leaving the disturbing sense that cruelty needs no good reason.

b.s: Small Things Like These ends with questions unanswered, as we never learn what happens to Sarah, Bill's daughters or his business.

link.why: Both endings refuse to tie everything up, leaving the audience or reader uneasy.

a.s: In Othello, the joy of the Cyprus reunion, when Othello says he could die 'most happy', ends with him putting out the light before he smothers Desdemona.

b.s: the darkness of the convent in Small Things Like These is broken by kindness, as Bill takes Sarah out of the coal shed and walks her home.

link.why: Shakespeare lets the darkness put out the light, while Keegan lets one act of kindness break through the dark.

a.s: Warden Norton keeps control through force, having Hadley shoot Tommy dead and threatening to destroy the library if Andy stops working for him.

b.s: than Norton, the Mother Superior keeps control through politeness, calling the night in the coal shed a game and hinting that places at the school are scarce.

link.why: Both institutions control people, but the convent works through hints while the prison uses open force.

a.s: In Small Things Like These, Bill has risen from nothing to owning a business, and he and Eileen fear losing their place by offending the nuns.

b.s: status in The Shawshank Redemption depends on the institution: inside, Brooks is the respected librarian, but outside he is an old man bagging groceries in a world with no use for him.

link.why: In both worlds a person's standing depends on a powerful institution, which can take it away.

a.s: In The Shawshank Redemption, the prisoners build their own community, and Red's group of friends becomes Andy's substitute family.

b.s: the community in Small Things Like These knows what goes on in the convent but looks away, and people avoid Bill as he walks Sarah through the town.

link.why: Darabont's prisoners stand by one another, while Keegan's townspeople turn their backs on anyone who disturbs the order.

a.s: Small Things Like These is hopeful about individuals but darker about society, since one man chooses to act while the town looks away.

b.s: Darabont's film suggests that institutions are corrupt but individuals can be good, as justice comes from Andy's patience and a newspaper, not from the courts.

link.why: Both texts place their hope in one good person rather than in the institutions around them.

a.s: The Shawshank Redemption ends in bright sunlight, as Red is reunited with Andy on a beach in Mexico and the camera pulls back over the blue Pacific.

b.s: than The Shawshank Redemption, Small Things Like These ends on hope: Bill reaches his door with Sarah, afraid but hopeful, and we never learn how Eileen or the town will respond.

link.why: Both endings are hopeful, but Keegan's open ending leaves the reader uneasy, while Darabont's reunion feels complete.

chains.title: Power in Othello, Sive and Shawshank
steps: In Othello, Sive and The Shawshank Redemption, real power often lies not with those who seem to be in charge but with those who can manipulate them.
In Othello, Iago, a mere ensign, works on his general through hints, pauses and pretended reluctance until Othello vows revenge and makes him his lieutenant.
Similarly, Mike is the man of the house in name only in Sive, as Mena, tempted by Seán Dóta's £200, works on him until he gives in to the match.
The Shawshank Redemption turns this around: unlike Iago and Mena, Andy, a mere prisoner, uses his financial skill against the corrupt warden, taking the money he had hidden for Norton.
Ultimately, hidden power destroys in Othello and Sive but frees Andy in Shawshank, and Othello is the bleakest of the three, since Iago never even explains why.

chains.title: Courage and silence in STLT, Othello and Shawshank
steps: All three texts show that silence protects the powerful, and that breaking it takes a courage which always comes at a cost.
In Small Things Like These, Bill finally breaks the town's silence on Christmas Eve, walking a barefoot Sarah home even though he knows he will pay for it.
Likewise, Emilia breaks her silence in Othello, defying her husband's order to hold her peace, but her courage costs her life when Iago stabs her.
Speaking out is punished just as harshly in The Shawshank Redemption, where Andy is thrown into solitary for challenging the warden and Tommy is shot for agreeing to testify.
Of the three, Keegan offers the most hopeful view of courage, since Bill's act brings him a happiness greater than any he has known.

chains.title: Women and marriage in Sive, Othello and STLT
steps: In all three worlds, a woman's worth is judged through marriage, and women who fall outside its rules, or are suspected of breaking them, are punished.
In Sive, Mena tells Sive she will have no name till she takes a husband, using her birth outside marriage as a weapon to force the match.
Marriage gives no protection in Othello either: Othello treats Desdemona as 'that cunning whore of Venice' and later smothers her, and Iago stabs Emilia for disobeying him.
Small Things Like These shows this punishment at its most systematic, as unmarried mothers like Sarah are locked away and their babies taken, while the shame never falls on the fathers.
Ultimately, all three expose a world where women pay for men's judgements, though only Keegan shows a man, Bill, refusing to look away.

chains.title: The Church in STLT, Shawshank and Sive
steps: In all three texts, religion serves power and respectability rather than protecting the vulnerable.
In Small Things Like These, the convent is admired for its beauty, yet behind its walls topped with broken glass girls are locked up and a young mother's baby is taken.
Similarly, in The Shawshank Redemption, Warden Norton greets new prisoners with talk of discipline and the Bible, yet he runs a corrupt business and arranges a murder.
Less overtly than either, the Church in Sive stands for respectability: when Sive drowns, Mike's first thought is whether she can be buried in holy ground.
Of the three, Keegan's criticism is the most direct, because the cruelty is carried out by the Church itself rather than merely in its name.

chains.title: Endings in Sive, STLT and Shawshank
steps: The endings of the three texts reveal very different visions: bleak in Sive, hopeful but uncertain in Small Things Like These, and triumphantly hopeful in The Shawshank Redemption.
Sive ends with a drowned girl, Carthalawn's lament and Nanna's grief, while the matchmaker and the bridegroom slip away and no one is brought to account.
In contrast, Small Things Like These ends with Bill walking Sarah home, feeling a happiness greater than any he has known, though we never learn how Eileen or the town responds.
The Shawshank Redemption goes further still, ending in bright sunlight as Red walks along the beach at Zihuatanejo to Andy and the camera pulls back over the blue Pacific.
Ultimately, the hope in these texts comes from individuals rather than society, which is why Sive, where goodness is powerless, leaves the bleakest vision of all.

chains.title: Light and dark in Othello, Shawshank and STLT
steps: All three texts set moments of light against darkness, but they differ sharply over which one wins.
In Othello, the joy of the Cyprus reunion, when Othello says he could die 'most happy', is destroyed when he puts out the light before smothering Desdemona.
In contrast, The Shawshank Redemption moves from grey prison walls and night scenes like Tommy's killing to the open, sunlit blue of the Pacific in its final shot.
Small Things Like These sits between the two, setting the warmth of the Furlong kitchen at Christmas against the girl locked all night in the convent's coal shed.
Ultimately, light is destroyed in Othello, triumphs in Shawshank and survives only uncertainly in Keegan's novella, which makes the film the most hopeful of the three.

lines: All three texts show that good people exist, but they differ sharply on whether goodness can survive.

In contrast, goodness cannot save itself in Othello, where Desdemona stays loyal to the end and Emilia dies when Othello stabs her for speaking out.
Sive is bleaker still, as the goodness of Liam, Nanna and the travelling men is powerless against the money that drives the match.
Ultimately, only Darabont lets goodness win, which is why his film feels hopeful while the two plays leave us with grief and pity.

lines: All three texts are set in societies where some people have more power than others.
In Othello, the Duke and Senate judge Brabantio's complaint, and a letter from Venice can recall even a great general.
In contrast, the real authority in Small Things Like These is the Catholic Church, and Bill understands the Mother Superior's remark that school places are scarce as a warning.
In Sive, authority belongs to whoever has money, as Seán Dóta's wealth buys him a bride and the matchmaker Thomasheen brokers the deal for his own gain.
Of the three worlds, Keegan's is the most frightening, because its power is never openly stated, yet the whole town defers to it.

lines: Each text opens in a dark or troubled world, but only Small Things Like These moves from that darkness towards hope.
Keane's play opens in a cramped, poor kitchen where Nanna and Mena trade insults, and Sive, home from school, is treated as a burden.
Othello also opens in darkness, at night, with Iago's hatred and racist shouts, though Othello's calm dignity before the Senate suggests that goodness may win out.
Small Things Like These starts with Bill doing his rounds, then the town gathers for the Christmas lights, and the Furlongs bake the Christmas cake at home.
Ultimately, both plays move from these dark openings to tragedy, while Keegan's muted start prepares for a hopeful, if uncertain, ending.

lines: In all three worlds, money shapes people's choices: it tempts the greedy, frightens the insecure and corrupts the powerful.
In Sive, poverty drives the tragedy, as Mena, who married to escape a desperately poor home, will not refuse Seán Dóta's £200.
Similarly, hard times in Small Things Like These make families cling to what they have, and Eileen argues that only wealth gave Mrs Wilson the freedom to be kind.
Worse still, in The Shawshank Redemption money corrupts the institution itself, as Captain Hadley relies on Andy to hide his illegal profits and so will not let Tommy's evidence set him free.
Of the three, Keegan shows most clearly how money buys silence, since fear of losing what they have keeps decent people quiet.

The Shawshank Redemption is a hopeful film, and Red ends it with the words 'I hope'.

lines: The most effective power in all three texts works quietly, through persuasion, knowledge and hints rather than force.
In Othello, Iago, a mere ensign, uses hints, pauses and pretended reluctance in the temptation scene until his general vows murderous revenge.
Similarly, Andy discovers in The Shawshank Redemption that knowledge is power, when his tax advice turns Captain Hadley from threatening him into supplying beer for his fellow prisoners.
More subtly still, the Mother Superior in Small Things Like These controls Bill's visit by calling the night in the coal shed a game and hinting that school places are scarce.
So power is a very important theme in all three texts and it affects all of the characters in different ways.

lines: The communities in all three texts shape who survives: chosen friendships protect people, while families and towns can turn their backs.
In The Shawshank Redemption, the prisoners build their own community, and Red's group of friends becomes Andy's substitute family, ending in a reunion in Mexico.
In Small Things Like These, Bill pays for his men's dinner on Christmas Eve, Mrs Kehoe asks him about the Mother Superior, and then he walks on to the convent.
In Othello, family ties break completely, as Brabantio disowns Desdemona, and far from home her only real companion is Emilia.
Of the three, Darabont offers the most hopeful view of community, since only his chosen family survives intact.

spot.ask: Tap the line an examiner wouldn't reward.
lines: Each writer or director shapes our outlook by controlling what we know, and so decides whether we finish in hope, dread or uncertainty.
In Small Things Like These, the nuns run the laundry and the best girls' school, so they have enormous power over the town.
In contrast, Shakespeare tells us too much in Othello: Iago reveals his plan in soliloquy while Othello calls him 'honest Iago', so we watch helplessly as disaster approaches.
Darabont, on the other hand, hides Andy's escape from the viewer as well as from Red, so its sudden reveal gives us the same shock and delight.
Ultimately, Shakespeare's dramatic irony creates the bleakest experience, while Darabont's surprise makes his vision the most uplifting of the three.
